hints: Focus on where the ammonia product must come from, and what has to happen to an ammonium ion to become ammonia.
Notice that $\text{NH}_4^+$ becomes $\text{NH}_3$ by losing a proton, so ask yourself what species must pick up that proton.
Connect proton accepting to the Bronsted-Lowry definition, and check whether any oxidation numbers change to rule out redox behaviour.
walkthrough:
**Write what happens on warming**

Think of this as ammonium salts breaking down to release ammonia. The ammonium ion must lose a proton to become ammonia.

Overall reaction:
$$ (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$

**Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definitions**

A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor, and a Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. Keep it simple: who gives $\text{H}^+$, who takes $\text{H}^+$?

Key change:
$$ \text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ $$

**See the role of carbonate**

That $\text{H}^+$ released by ammonium cannot just disappear. The carbonate ion picks it up to form hydrogencarbonate and then water plus carbon dioxide.

Proton acceptance:
$$ \text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- $$

**Rule out oxidation and reduction**

Check oxidation numbers. N stays at -3 in $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NH}_3$, and C stays at +4 in $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ and $\text{CO}_2$. No electron gain or loss occurs, so this is an acid-base reaction, with carbonate acting as the base.

options.A: Incorrect. The Bronsted-Lowry acid is the proton donor, which is $\text{NH}_4^+$, not $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$. Carbonate accepts the proton rather than donating it.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ donates a proton to become $\text{NH}_3$, and $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ accepts that proton to form $\text{HCO}_3^-$ (then $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). Accepting a proton is exactly Bronsted-Lowry base behaviour.
options.C: Incorrect. An oxidising agent gains electrons and causes oxidation numbers to change. Here N remains -3 and C remains +4, so no redox occurs.
options.D: Incorrect. A reducing agent loses electrons and causes oxidation numbers to change. No element changes oxidation number in this thermal decomposition, so carbonate is not acting as a reducing agent.
